interest: This file offers valuable historical insight into the escalating bureaucratic and diplomatic warfare between Japan, the United States, and Great Britain in late summer 1941, just months prior to the outbreak of the Pacific War following the July 1941 freezing of Japanese assets. It vividly documents the labyrinthine administrative obstacles and catch-22 regulations imposed by Japanese authorities on departing foreign nationals—spanning exit permits, multi-tiered exchange approvals, advance tax assessments, and liquidation restrictions. Crucially, Frank Schuler's State Department memorandum reveals how U.S. officials compared these stringent Japanese exit barriers against much more permissive American procedures, actively evaluating whether to invoke diplomatic reciprocity to restrict departing Japanese nationals.
overview: This file from the Department of State Decimal File 894.56 (Internal Affairs of Japan: Emigration) covers the period from August 22 to September 16, 1941, and concerns the restrictive regulations imposed by the Japanese government on foreigners seeking to depart Japan, as well as a comparative assessment of United States departure regulations for Japanese nationals. The file centers on an August 30, 1941 telegram extract from London transmitted via the British Embassy describing the extensive web of permits (prefectural exit permits, foreign exchange permits, income tax clearances, ticket purchase permits, and business liquidation approvals) required of 'designated foreigners' leaving Japan. In response, Division of Far Eastern Affairs officer Frank A. Schuler, Jr. prepared a comparative memorandum for Assistant Secretary of State Dean Acheson demonstrating that American requirements were far fewer and simpler, while noting that existing regulations provided ample basis for reciprocal restrictions against Japanese nationals if desired. The file also preserves an incomplete copy of the British extract and a cross-reference sheet to a related August 22, 1941 despatch from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo.

subfiles.about: A Department of State memorandum comparing restrictive Japanese departure controls on foreigners with the far simpler American regulations applied to departing Japanese nationals.
subfiles.from: Frank A. Schuler, Jr. (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Drafted by Frank A. Schuler, Jr. in the Division of Far Eastern Affairs for Assistant Secretary Dean Acheson, this memorandum responds to information received from the British regarding Japanese departure requirements for foreigners. Drawing on information from the Visa Division and Alger Hiss, Schuler provides a point-by-point comparison showing that the United States does not require exit permits, baggage permits, ticket purchase authorizations, or special liquidation permits for departing Japanese nationals. The memorandum concludes that U.S. procedures are significantly simpler and less onerous, but highlights that existing American regulations could provide a legal basis for establishing reciprocal restrictions against departing Japanese nationals if the U.S. government chooses to do so.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Frank A. Schuler, Jr. comparing American and Japanese departure requirements

subfiles.about: An incomplete copy of an extract of a British telegram describing the extensive administrative permits required for foreigners seeking to depart Japan.
subfiles.from: British Foreign Office / British Embassy (Mr. Denning)
subfiles.summary: This document is a single-page, incomplete copy of an extract of a telegram sent from London on August 30, 1941, and delivered by Mr. Denning of the British Embassy to Mr. Adams of the State Department on September 8, 1941. It outlines the onerous requirements imposed on 'designated foreigners' leaving Japan, including prefectural exit permits, multiple foreign exchange permits, receipts for taxes and employee retirement allowances, and permits to buy travel tickets and liquidate assets. The document breaks off in paragraph 5 while discussing the difficulty of obtaining official application forms outside Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Incomplete extract of a telegram from London on Japanese departure regulations
subfiles.to: Mr. Adams (Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State)

subfiles.about: A complete two-page British telegram extract detailing the elaborate permit process, financial restrictions, and administrative obstacles confronting foreigners departing Japan.
subfiles.from: British Foreign Office / British Embassy (Mr. Denning)
subfiles.summary: This document contains the complete two-page text of the telegram extract from London dated August 30, 1941, handed to Mr. Adams at the State Department on September 8, 1941. It details the extensive bureaucratic hurdles designated foreigners face when attempting to leave Japan, including securing exit permits from prefectural governors, multiple exchange permits from designated banks, receipts for income taxes and staff allowances, ticket purchase permits, baggage release permits, and property liquidation licenses. It emphasizes that fulfilling tax and financial obligations does not guarantee an exit permit, forms are nearly unobtainable outside Tokyo, and officials provide no guidance or reliable timelines for application processing.
subfiles.title: Extract of a telegram from London regarding Japanese regulations for the departure of foreigners
subfiles.to: Mr. Adams (Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State)

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet indexing a Tokyo despatch from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew concerning Japanese emigration matters.
subfiles.summary: This State Department cross-reference sheet references Despatch No. 5801 dated August 22, 1941, sent by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew from Japan. The original document is filed under decimal classification 894.111/100, which pertains to the status and movement of aliens and foreigners. The sheet places the reference into decimal file 894.56, the State Department category for Japanese internal affairs concerning emigration.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 5801 from Ambassador Grew
